7.2 Special look at Suzone Level (Geylang East)

Ripley’s L(r) – r for Subzone Spatial Clustering

This chunk computes and plots Ripley’s L(r) – r for the second most active subzone of a chosen sector (default: IT (62)), to assess within-subzone spatial clustering.

  • Pick target subzone:
    Count points by SUBZONE_N for the sector, sort by frequency, and select the 2nd highest (sz2).
    This avoids an over-dominant hotspot while still analysing a busy area.

  • Build point pattern in that subzone:

    • to_ppp_in() converts the subzone polygon to an owin window.
    • The sector’s points in that subzone are converted to a ppp object x.

  • Choose analysis range:

    • Set rmax to the smaller of 1200 m or half the subzone diameter (guard against edge artefacts).
    • Create r_seq every 25 m.

  • Compute L-function:

    • Use spatstat.explore::Lest() with Ripley’s correction.
    • Build a dataframe with ( L(r) - r ), where 0 indicates CSR (Complete Spatial Randomness).

  • Plot:

    • Line plot of ( L(r) - r ) vs ( r ) with a dashed 0-line.
    • Title includes the sector and subzone.
# sector to analyse (change if needed), or loop over your `sectors`
sec <- "IT (62)"

# find the 2nd most active subzone for this sector
sz_counts <- biz_pts_use |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::filter(sector == sec) |>
  dplyr::count(SUBZONE_N, name = "n") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n))

stopifnot(nrow(sz_counts) >= 2)
sz2 <- sz_counts$SUBZONE_N[2]; n2 <- sz_counts$n[2]
message("Sector: ", sec, " | 2nd subzone: ", sz2, " (n=", n2, ")")

# build ppp in that subzone
to_ppp_in <- function(pts_sf, poly_sf){
  Wsz <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(poly_sf)
  xy  <- sf::st_coordinates(pts_sf)
  spatstat.geom::ppp(xy[,1], xy[,2], window = Wsz, check = FALSE)
}
pts_sz <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == sec, SUBZONE_N == sz2)
poly_sz <- dplyr::filter(subzones_use, SUBZONE_N == sz2)
X <- to_ppp_in(pts_sz, poly_sz)

# L(r)-r (cap range to half the subzone diameter, max 1200 m)
rmax <- min(1200, spatstat.geom::diameter.owin(spatstat.geom::Window(X))/2)
r_seq <- seq(0, rmax, by = 25)
L     <- spatstat.explore::Lest(X, r = r_seq, correction = "Ripley")
dfL   <- as.data.frame(L) |>
  dplyr::transmute(r = r, LminusR = iso - r)

ggplot2::ggplot(dfL, ggplot2::aes(r, LminusR)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = paste0(sec, " — ", sz2, " (2nd most active)"),
    subtitle = "Ripley L(r) − r within subzone window",
    x = "r (m)", y = "L(r) − r"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Thematic Map of the 2nd Most Active Subzone (IT 62)

This block creates a thematic map of the 2nd most active subzone for the IT (62) sector, highlighting the subzone polygon and the business registration points inside it.

  • Data prep:
    • pts_sz: all IT registrations within the chosen subzone (sz2).
    • poly_sz: polygon geometry for that subzone.
    • bbox_sz: bounding box padded (≈400 m) around the subzone for map spacing.
  • Mapping steps with tmap:
    1. Background: plot all planning subzones (subzones_use) within the bounding box, filled light grey (grey95) with thin white borders.
    2. Highlight subzone: overlay the target polygon in light yellow (#FFE082), semi-transparent, with an orange border (#F57F17). Label with SUBZONE_N.
    3. Points: overlay all IT registrations (pts_sz) as small steel-blue dots, semi-transparent for clarity.
    4. Layout: add a title showing sector, subzone name, and registration count; hide legend; remove frame; fix scaling for a clean appearance.
library(tmap)

# Sector + 2nd most active subzone (you already computed sz2)
sec    <- "IT (62)"
pts_sz <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == sec, SUBZONE_N == sz2)
poly_sz <- dplyr::filter(subzones_use, SUBZONE_N == sz2)

# a slightly padded bbox so the subzone has breathing room
bbox_sz <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_buffer(sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(poly_sz)), 400))

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(subzones_use, bbox = bbox_sz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey95", border.col = "white") +
tm_shape(poly_sz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "#FFE082", alpha = 0.6, border.col = "#F57F17", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", size = 0.9, col = "black", auto.placement = TRUE) +  # <-- on polygon
tm_shape(pts_sz) +
  tm_dots(col = "steelblue", size = 0.2, alpha = 0.55) +
tm_layout(
  title = sprintf("%s — %s (%d registrations)", sec, sz2, nrow(pts_sz)),
  legend.show = FALSE, frame = FALSE, component.autoscale = FALSE
)

The L(r) − r curve is strongly above 0 at short distances, peaking within ~50–250 m, then declines and crosses 0 around ~850 m. Interpretation: IT registrations are clustered at block–neighbourhood scales (tens to a few hundred metres). Beyond ~0.8 km the pattern is no longer more clustered than CSR; the slight negatives likely reflect edge effects/land-use gaps rather than true repulsion.

The map shows many points concentrated within the subzone, forming several tight mini-clusters rather than a uniform spread—consistent with co-location in business buildings, coworking floors, or along commercial corridors.

Planning takeaway: support small-footprint, flexible office space and amenities within walkable (≤800 m) catchments; monitoring should focus on these local nodes rather than wider-area interventions.

For other sectors This code defines reusable helpers to analyze and visualize business clustering within a chosen subzone. plot_Lr_for_subzone() builds a point pattern inside the subzone and plots Ripley’s L(r) − r to assess clustering vs. CSR, while map_sector_subzone() produces a clean thematic map highlighting the subzone and its business registration points.

# build ppp inside a subzone polygon
to_ppp_in <- function(pts_sf, poly_sf){
  Wsz <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(poly_sf)
  xy  <- sf::st_coordinates(pts_sf)
  spatstat.geom::ppp(xy[,1], xy[,2], window = Wsz, check = FALSE)
}

# L(r) - r plot inside a subzone
plot_Lr_for_subzone <- function(sec, sz_name, by = 25, r_cap = 1200){
  pts_sz  <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == sec, SUBZONE_N == sz_name)
  poly_sz <- dplyr::filter(subzones_use,  SUBZONE_N == sz_name)
  stopifnot(nrow(poly_sz) == 1, nrow(pts_sz) > 0)

  X <- to_ppp_in(pts_sz, poly_sz)
  rmax <- min(r_cap, spatstat.geom::diameter.owin(spatstat.geom::Window(X))/2)
  L    <- spatstat.explore::Lest(X, r = seq(0, rmax, by = by), correction = "Ripley")
  dfL  <- as.data.frame(L) |> dplyr::transmute(r = r, LminusR = iso - r)

  ggplot2::ggplot(dfL, ggplot2::aes(r, LminusR)) +
    ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = sprintf("%s — %s", sec, sz_name),
      subtitle = "Ripley L(r) − r within subzone window",
      x = "r (m)", y = "L(r) − r"
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()
}

# clean subzone map with points
map_sector_subzone <- function(sec, sz_name){
  pts_sz  <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == sec, SUBZONE_N == sz_name)
  poly_sz <- dplyr::filter(subzones_use,  SUBZONE_N == sz_name)
  bbox_sz <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_buffer(sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(poly_sz)), 400))

  tmap_mode("plot")
  tm_shape(subzones_use, bbox = bbox_sz) + tm_polygons(col = "grey95", border.col = "white") +
  tm_shape(poly_sz) + tm_polygons(col = "#FFE082", alpha = 0.6, border.col = "#F57F17", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", size = 0.9, col = "black", auto.placement = TRUE) +
  tm_shape(pts_sz) + tm_dots(col = "steelblue", size = 0.2, alpha = 0.55) +
  tm_layout(
    title = sprintf("%s — %s (%d registrations)", sec, sz_name, nrow(pts_sz)),
    legend.show = FALSE, frame = FALSE, component.autoscale = FALSE
  )
}
sz_name <- "GEYLANG EAST"

# F&B (56)
print(plot_Lr_for_subzone("F&B (56)", sz_name))
print(map_sector_subzone("F&B (56)", sz_name))

F&B (56) — Geylang East (subzone)

The subzone K-function ( L(r) - r ) is strongly positive from 0–~750 m, peaking at very short ranges (tens of metres) and tapering steadily.

This means new F&B registrations are clustered at block–neighbourhood scales, consistent with mall/market streets and MRT-proximate shopfronts.

The curve crosses ~0 around 0.75–0.8 km, indicating that beyond this radius the pattern is no more clustered than random within the subzone.

The mild negative tail after ~900–1100 m is typical of edge effects as distances approach the subzone’s diameter, not true repulsion. The map corroborates several micro-clusters spread across GEYLANG EAST rather than a single node.

Planning note: street-management and licensing hotspots are likely within ≤500–800 m corridors; improvements to pedestrian flow and cleaning/enforcement should prioritise these clusters.

# Logistics/Warehousing (52)
print(plot_Lr_for_subzone("Logistics/Warehousing (52)", sz_name))
print(map_sector_subzone("Logistics/Warehousing (52)", sz_name))

Ripley’s ( L(r) - r ) inside the subzone is strongly positive at very small radii (peak < 50 m), meaning registrations tend to co-locate in the same or adjacent buildings—typical of multi-tenant warehouses or repeated use of a few addresses.

The curve declines steadily and crosses ~0 at ~0.85–0.9 km, then becomes negative out to ~1.2 km, indicating spacing between clusters at estate scale (i.e., once you move ~1 km away, new firms are less likely than random to appear there, given the subzone window).

The dot map (≈105 registrations) shows few, tight nodes along main corridors and very little presence elsewhere, consistent with zoning and frontage access needs.

Planning takeaways:
- Focus servicing/curb and loading management around those micro-clusters.
- Preserve small-parcel/strata industrial supply.
- Interpret cautiously since registrations may reflect office/registered addresses rather than operational sites.

8 Final Planning Summary

New business registrations in Singapore during 2025-H1 (with 2024 as baseline) reveal distinct spatial logics by sector and common temporal rhythms that matter for planning, infrastructure and place management. F&B (SSIC 56) exhibits an island-wide footprint with dense, walk-scale clusters in the CBD/fringe-CBD and town-centre/MRT nodes. KDE peaks around transit-rich malls and mixed-use corridors; subzone L(r)–r curves are positive up to ~750–800 m, indicating neighbourhood-scale agglomeration. Policy levers here are placemaking and curb/servicing management rather than land-supply: concentrate cleaning, licensing and pedestrian flow improvements in ≤800 m corridors around the highest-intensity nodes; monitor saturation to avoid nuisance spillovers into residential streets.

IT services (SSIC 62) are both widely dispersed and highly concentrated at a few office ecosystems—CBD, one-north, Changi Business Park, Tampines/Jurong regional hubs. The nearest-neighbour test shows the strongest clustering among the three sectors, consistent with co-location in towers, business parks and coworking floors. Yet the space–time K surfaces are largely flat at short lags, with significance appearing at ~1.5 km / ~90 days, suggesting quarterly, estate-scale bursts (lease cycles, batch incorporations) rather than week-to-week contagion. Planning actions: ensure flexible office stock and grade-A to flexible B1 spaces near rapid transit; streamline fit-out and data/telecom permitting on a quarterly cadence; and enhance last-mile public transport between parks and MRT to widen the catchment of talent and services.

Logistics/Warehousing (SSIC 52) is sparse but decisive, tracking industrial corridors and gateways (Jurong/Tuas, port-proximity zones, and the Changi axis). KDE shows a long-tailed distribution: large low-intensity background with few, very high-intensity estate nodes. Subzone L(r)–r indicates micro-co-location (<50 m peaks) inside multi-tenant warehouses and a decline beyond ~0.85–0.9 km, implying estate-scale spacing. Space–time K again flags quarter-year pulses at ~1.5 km, consistent with phased openings and coordinated leases. Implications: preserve a pipeline of industrial parcels with good expressway access, protect loading/servicing capacity, and manage last-mile interfaces where estates abut residential areas (noise, heavy-vehicle routing, staging).

Cross-cutting, three themes emerge. First, registered-office effects inflate CBD counts; planners should triangulate KDE hotspots with operational land-use (e.g., mall/food clusters vs. office-mailing addresses) to calibrate interventions. Second, the space–time signal at ~quarterly intervals argues for batch-oriented permitting and monitoring—monthly dashboards are useful but quarterly capacity checks better match market rhythm. Third, transit adjacency consistently underpins intensity across sectors: prioritising walkability and MRT connectivity around mixed-use hubs yields the broadest spillovers (jobs, services, footfall).

In short, F&B needs fine-grain, street-scale management; IT requires flexible, transit-served office ecosystems; and Logistics depends on protected industrial estates with robust access. Aligning licensing, infrastructure, and space supply to these scales—and reviewing them on a quarterly cycle—will sustain growth while mitigating over-concentration risks.
